newsitem.title: UK: UK Conservatives' re-election hopes take big blow.
newsitem.headline: UK Conservatives' re-election hopes take big blow.

text.p: Britain's ruling Conservatives were staring into the abyss on Friday after a convincing by-election victory left Tony Blair's opposition Labour party firmly on course to win the coming general election.
Prime Minister John Major told a television interviewer: "if opinion does not change then we are going to have a Labour government."

Labour candidate Ben Chapman stormed home in the affluent commuter-belt constituency of Wirral South, north-west England, overturning a Conservative majority of 8,183 votes to win by a margin of 7,888 votes.
Chapman polled 53 percent of the vote as Labour enjoyed a 17 percent swing -- dwarfing the 4.3 percent swing it would need to win the general election, widely expected to be held on May 1.

Major -- who on Friday became Britain's fourth-longest serving prime minister this century -- is now in a minority in parliament, having 322 seats compared with 323 for the combined opposition. But Labour accept they have little chance of triggering an early election because Major has the support of nine Protestant Ulster Unionist MPs from Northern Ireland.
The pound dipped a pfennig against the German mark in early trade after the result but had recovered its losses by mid-day to stand around 2.75 marks.
If the Wirral South result, which was broadly in line with national opinion polls, were repeated at the general election, Labour would win by a landslide.

The Conservatives had been braced for defeat, but not by such a wide margin, and could not even fall back on the excuse that their voters had stayed at home. The total turnout was 73 percent, high for a by-election.
In the by-election, caused by the death of Conservative Barry Porter, Chapman polled 22,767 votes to Conservative Les Byrom's 14,879 with the minority Liberal Democrats on 4,357.
Labour, in opposition since 1979, was jubilant. "For Tories to dismiss this as a protest vote simply confirms how out of touch and arrogant they are," Blair said.
His aides noted that no party in Britain's recent history had closed a deficit of the size the Conservatives now face in the two months that probably remain before the general election.

"One thing is absolutely clear -- this is an extremely bad result for the Conservatives and anyone who tries to pretend otherwise is deluding themselves," David Mellor a former Conservative cabinet minister, told Sky Television.
Pro-Conservative newspapers added to the ruling party's gloom. "The spectre of a general election defeat was haunting John Major today," The Express said in its lead report.
The Daily Telegraph said Conservative hopes of a fifth straight term in office had been dealt "a massive blow".

The significance of the result for Labour is that Wirral South is a microcosm of middle England that is a natural home to the sort of prosperous and aspiring Conservative-minded voters Blair has methodically wooed since he became leader in 1994.
Blair has sought to bury Labour's tax-and-spend image while promising to improve education and health and to reverse most of the Conservatives' sweeping industrial and union reforms.
Wirral South shows the message seems to be getting across.
Although polls failed to predict Major's win in 1992, Labour enjoyed only a slender lead in the run-up to the election.
Now Labour is some 20 points ahead and has momentum whereas voters view the Conservatives, deeply divided over Europe, as accident-prone and short of fresh ideas after 18 years in power.

"We have never treated any general election as being sewn up. We've lost four elections," Labour's deputy leader John Prescott said as he celebrated with Chapman at a champagne breakfast. "But we now think there is the best chance we have ever had."
